Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: MetricsAbsent on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: No metrics received from io-shop since 2026-10-26T10:30:00Z {A1} - 5m {A2} with no sample, against a scrape interval of 15 {A3} seconds. The series stopped rather than crossing a threshold, so nothing here says whether the shop is well: these minutes have no readings to judge, not readings that look bad.
Alert raised: 2026-10-26T10:35:44Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 5 minutes 44 seconds {alerted_after_the_onset} after the onset.
No metrics were collected from 2026-10-26T10:30:00Z {metrics_stopped_at} (the onset) onwards: the metrics had still not resumed by 2026-10-26T10:39:16Z {argus_stopped}. That is 9 minutes 16 seconds {duration} the metrics did not cover, not a stretch the service is known to have spent in trouble.
Log lines read reach into it until 2026-10-26T10:35:00Z {logs_reach_until}: [G46bc], [Gbac1], [Gad41]. They are the service's own account of that stretch: what they report there is what is known of how it was doing, and up to then the service was seen through them. The logs were read up to 2026-10-26T10:35:42Z {log_reading_ended} - nothing after that was read.
How the service did over that stretch is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before: say nothing of it anywhere else. Where the chain's first step says nobody using the service saw anything wrong, cite those log lines for it without saying what they show.
Argus held the incident for 3 minutes 31 seconds {held}, until 2026-10-26T10:39:16Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - none were collected after the metrics stopped; the log lines that reach into that stretch, [G46bc], [Gbac1], [Gad41], are the service's own account of it, so do not say nothing was measured; what they show is said by the document itself, from your answer to logs_show_serving_as_before.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-10-26T10:35:45Z {T1.1} Argus: Received MetricsAbsent on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-10-26T10:36:05Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-10-26T10:36:06Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-10-26T10:36:21Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 10:35:44 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-10-26T10:36:53Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read the service's metrics - they stop after the minute at 10:29 {T5.2}, and nothing covers the minutes since
  - [T6] 2026-10-26T10:36:54Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 10:30 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-10-26T10:36:54Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-10-26T10:36:56Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 5 {T8.3} minutes 44 {T8.4} seconds before Oct 26 10:35:44 {T8.5}
  - [T9] 2026-10-26T10:36:57Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 2 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-10-26T10:36:57Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 7 {T10.2} minutes 42 {T10.3} seconds before 10:35:42 {T10.4}
  - [T11] 2026-10-26T10:36:58Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 18 {T11.2} log lines
  - [T12] 2026-10-26T10:37:05Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read what the deployment of c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 changed
  - [T13] 2026-10-26T10:37:05Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T13.2} replicas run revision c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3, deployed at 10:30 {T13.3}
  - [T14] 2026-10-26T10:37:06Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 2 {T14.2} candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
  - [T15] 2026-10-26T10:37:06Z {T15.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T16] 2026-10-26T10:37:07Z {T16.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T16.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T16.3} hour before 10:37:06 {T16.4}
  - [T17] 2026-10-26T10:37:13Z {T17.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on the leading candidate
  - [T18] 2026-10-26T10:37:13Z {T18.1} Argus: Refused to act - the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose
  - [T19] 2026-10-26T10:37:13Z {T19.1} Argus: Moved the incident to FIXING - no mitigation taken
  - [T20] 2026-10-26T10:39:16Z {T20.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/358
  - [T21] 2026-10-26T10:39:16Z {T21.1} Argus: Moved the incident to ESCALATED - a draft pull request is open at https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/358

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-10-26T06:30:00Z {P1.1} deploy 2c8f7311966cf37dee314695fe0060867e1ca954 by kuki: deployed revision 2c8f7311966cf37dee314695fe0060867e1ca954 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - [P2] 2026-10-26T10:30:00Z {P2.1} deploy c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 by kuki: deployed revision c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
  - Flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - before the metrics stopped: 2 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 1 {G46bc.2} minute, 10:28 {G46bc.3}. After they stopped: 8 {G46bc.4} occurrences in 6 {G46bc.5} minutes, 10:30–10:35 {G46bc.6}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - before the metrics stopped: 1 {Gbac1.1} occurrence in 1 {Gbac1.2} minute, 10:28 {Gbac1.3}; # was 1.00 {Gbac1.4}. After they stopped: 5 {Gbac1.5} occurrences in 6 {Gbac1.6} minutes, 10:30–10:35 {Gbac1.7}; # was 0.50 {Gbac1.8} to 1.50 {Gbac1.9}, typically 1.00 {Gbac1.10}, highest at 10:32 {Gbac1.11}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - before the metrics stopped: 1 {Gad41.1} occurrence in 1 {Gad41.2} minute, 10:29 {Gad41.3}. After they stopped: 1 {Gad41.4} occurrence in 1 {Gad41.5} minute, 10:33 {Gad41.6}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - cite them; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of deploy/values-production.yaml:ports.metrics.portName, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: The deployment at 2026-10-26T10:30:00Z {C1.1} deliberately renamed every port to the platform's `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` convention, including the metrics port (`metrics` to `http-metrics`). The monitoring scrape still selects the old name, so samples stopped. The shop kept serving normally. [monitoring-configuration-drift, confidence 0.8 {C1.2}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]
      C2: The revision changed one value, the metrics port name, so the scrape no longer finds it. Reverting would restore the metrics. The rename follows a convention applied across all three ports, which makes drift the better reading. [monitoring-blind-spot, confidence 0.15 {C1.3}, never tried: the only action that would test the candidate undoes a change that was made on purpose]

Actions it took:
  - none

What each deployment it looked into changed:
  - [D1] Deployment of revision c3c36da3c66c07707f227b7e70b26813083061f3 to io-shop, compared against 2c8f7311966cf37dee314695fe0060867e1ca954 - the revision deployed before it.
      modified deploy/values-production.yaml
        @@ -31,16 +31,19 @@ autoscaling:
           scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0 {D1.1}
         
         # The ports the shop serves on, each selected by name rather than number.
        +#
        +# Every port is named for the protocol it carries, then what it is for:
        +# `<protocol>[-<purpose>]`. The platform's convention, applied estate-wide.
         ports:
           web:
             port: 8000 {D1.2}
        -    portName: web
        +    portName: http
           admin:
             port: 8081 {D1.3}
        -    portName: admin
        +    portName: http-admin
           metrics:
             port: 9090 {D1.4}
        -    portName: metrics
        +    portName: http-metrics
         
         # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
         #
  - A file [D1] does not list is as it was at the revision [D1] compares against.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] What I read is main. Revision c3c36da, the one that ran, is not in main's history, so I have not seen it. I am relying on the investigation's account of its diff (metrics -> http-metrics).
      
      On main, `deploy/values-production.yaml` sets `metrics.portName: http-metrics`. On main, the ServiceMonitor in `deploy/scrape.yaml` selects its endpoint with `port: metrics`. The header comment in `deploy/scrape.yaml` says the scrape picks the target by the port's name, and that "a name that matches no port is not an error to the operator, it is a target list with nothing in it". So once the port was renamed, the scrape found no targets and samples stopped. The shop kept serving, as the logs show. The rename was a deliberate, platform-wide convention, so rolling it back is not the fix. The fault is that the scrape config lagged behind it and nothing checked the two against each other.
      
      The change:
      - `deploy/scrape.yaml`: `port: metrics` becomes `port: http-metrics`, so it matches the port name main's values file gives. Nothing else in the file changes.
      - New test `tests/io_shop/test_deploy_config.py`: it reads `metrics.portName` from `deploy/values-production.yaml` and every `port:` entry under the ServiceMonitor's `endpoints` in `deploy/scrape.yaml`, and asserts they are the same name. It parses both files with plain line scanning, so it doesn't need a YAML library. Against main's `deploy/scrape.yaml` before this change, it should fail (`metrics` != `http-metrics`). With the change it should pass. A future rename that touches only one of the two files would fail the test before merge. No test runner was available, so none of this has been run.
      
      Caveat: this fixes the config in the repository. Whoever deploys still has to apply the updated ServiceMonitor (or redeploy the chart from a branch that includes it). If c3c36da's branch has its own copy of `deploy/scrape.yaml`, it needs the same one-line change.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names revision c3c36da and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] deploy/scrape.yaml at c3c36da
      # How the platform's Prometheus collects the shop's metrics.
      #
      # It selects the shop's Service by label, then the endpoint to scrape on that
      # Service by the port's *name* - never its number - so a port can move without
      # anything here being touched.
      #
      # The name here has to be the one `metrics.portName` in values-production.yaml
      # gives the port. Nothing checks that the two agree: a name that matches no port
      # is not an error to the operator, it is a target list with nothing in it.
      apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
      kind: ServiceMonitor
      metadata:
        name: io-shop
        labels:
          release: prometheus
      spec:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            app: io-shop
        endpoints:
          - port: metrics
            path: /metrics
            interval: 15s {S1.1}
      
  - [S2] deploy/values-production.yaml at c3c36da
      # Deployment configuration for the io-shop account service, production.
      #
      # Rendered into the cluster as a ConfigMap and mounted into the pod, which is
      # why the service reads this file rather than being handed environment
      # variables: the values here are the deployment's, not the code's, and changing
      # one is a change to configuration that ships without the service being rebuilt.
      #
      # Owned by whoever runs the shop. Changes here go out the way any other change
      # goes out - reviewed, merged, and synced by the platform - and land without a
      # single line of io-shop's source being touched.
      
      replicas: 3 {S2.1}
      
      resources:
        memoryLimitMiB: 2048 {S2.2}
      
      # How the platform scales the shop.
      #
      # Rendered into a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, so `replicas` above is only where the
      # deployment starts: the controller decides the count from there, between the
      # floor and the ceiling here, aiming to keep each replica at the CPU target.
      #
      # `scaleDownStabilizationSeconds` is how far back the controller looks before it
      # believes a fall in load is real. Kubernetes defaults it to 300 {S2.3} - five minutes
      # of the highest recommendation it saw - because a controller acting on the
      # reading in front of it acts on a reading its own last action produced.
      autoscaling:
        minReplicas: 3 {S2.4}
        maxReplicas: 6 {S2.5}
        targetCpuPercent: 70 {S2.6}
        scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0 {S2.7}
      
      # The ports the shop serves on, each selected by name rather than number.
      #
      # Every port is named for the protocol it carries, then what it is for:
      # `<protocol>[-<purpose>]`. The platform's convention, applied estate-wide.
      ports:
        web:
          port: 8000 {S2.8}
          portName: http
        admin:
          port: 8081 {S2.9}
          portName: http-admin
        metrics:
          port: 9090 {S2.10}
          portName: http-metrics
      
      # Where the rendered-summary cache lives.
      #
      # The account page reads this cache before it works a shopper's spend figure
      # out, and recomputes when the cache has nothing or cannot be reached. So the
      # shop stays correct whatever is written here - it only stays *fast* while the
      # address is right.
      cache:
        host: cache.io-shop.svc.cluster.local
        port: 6380 {S2.11}
      

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #358 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P2] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Deploy a revision that carries the corrected deploy/scrape.yaml selecting `http-metrics`. Revision c3c36da's own scrape.yaml still selects `metrics`, and PR #358 was written against main, so the change has to be on the branch that actually deploys.
Run the port-name agreement test proposed in PR #358 as a required pre-merge check on every change under deploy/.
Add an alert or rollout gate that fires when io-shop's ServiceMonitor resolves to no scrape targets.
Route MetricsAbsent on io-shop to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
Check the scrape configurations of other services that adopted the estate-wide `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` port naming for selectors that still use old port names.

causal_chain.step: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong. What was seen instead was that the shop's metrics stopped after the minute at {T5.2} and no samples arrived after that, which raised MetricsAbsent.

The metrics stopped because the scrape found no target. The ServiceMonitor that ran picks the endpoint to scrape by the port name `metrics`, but the running values file names the metrics port `http-metrics`. The ServiceMonitor's own header says that a name matching no port is not an error to the operator but a target list with nothing in it.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 2c8f7311966cf37dee314695fe0060867e1ca954 at {P1.1}: the shop's metrics were still being collected with it in place, up to the minute at {T5.2}.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider showed {T16.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus in the {T16.3} hour before {T16.4}, and no flags came back when read.

causal_chain.step: No port was named `metrics` because the deploy of revision c3c36da at {P2.1} changed the metrics port's portName from `metrics` to `http-metrics` (and the web and admin ports to `http` and `http-admin`) in deploy/values-production.yaml only. The diff shows no change to deploy/scrape.yaml, so the scrape kept selecting the old name. As of {T13.1}, every replica was running revision c3c36da.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A configuration change renamed the port the shop publishes its measurements on, but the monitoring system still looked for the old name, so it stopped finding the shop and stopped collecting its measurements.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing checks that the port name the ServiceMonitor selects matches `metrics.portName` in the values file; the scrape configuration says so itself. No check of the two files against each other was seen on the change that renamed the port.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A rename that touched only the values file would have been caught before it shipped, and the scrape would have kept finding its target.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: A scrape whose target list is empty is not reported as an error to the operator. The fault was found only when the MetricsAbsent alert saw the series go missing.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The empty target list would have been flagged when the rollout happened, instead of only after the series had been missing for the alert's window.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: MetricsAbsent on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been told as soon as the alert fired and could have made the scrape-configuration change that Argus would not make, shortening the time without metrics.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well: Argus confirmed that every replica was running revision c3c36da {T13.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, and it had already read that revision's diff, which shows the metrics port rename.
Argus declined to roll back a change that was made on purpose to test the leading candidate, rather than undoing a deliberate platform-wide rename.
Code-Fix opened draft PR #358 {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, proposing a change to deploy/scrape.yaml and a new test.
went_wrong: Code-Fix read main, which does not contain the running revision c3c36da, so its proposal was written against a revision other than the one that ran. The same change is needed on whichever branch deploys.

input.root_cause: Revision c3c36da renamed the metrics port in deploy/values-production.yaml from `metrics` to `http-metrics` to follow the platform's `<protocol>[-<purpose>]` naming convention. The ServiceMonitor in deploy/scrape.yaml at the same revision still picks its scrape endpoint by the port name `metrics`. Because no port has that name any more, Prometheus's target list for the shop is empty, and that is not reported as an error, so no samples are collected.
input.still_at_risk: The running scrape configuration still looked for a port name that no port in the running deployment had, so the shop's metrics would stay uncollected, and any real trouble in the shop would not show in them or in the alerts built on them.
input.symptom: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong; the shop's metrics stopped arriving

content.content:
Your postmortem was not accepted:
  - the root_cause names [c3c36da] by its revision - the document states which change set it off; say why that change broke the service

Call submit_postmortem again with the whole answer, corrected.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label you cite (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed. Not how the service did over a stretch its metrics did not cover, nor what a failure there would have done - the document says how it did.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence: "Argus confirmed, {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, that the rollback had brought the service back", not "Argus confirmed the rollback had brought the service back from the incident's level {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised". Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

logs_show_serving_as_before.description: Whether the log lines that reach into the stretch the metrics did not watch show the service serving as it had before the metrics stopped. The document writes that sentence itself, bounded to when the logs were read.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself, after your sentence and a 'while', so end on what went wrong, with no clause after it - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.
